title: If a vulnerable person goes missing: what to prepare and what to do
lede: When a disappearance is concerning, there is no need to wait 24 hours. The response should take account of the missing person's age, health, communication, autonomy and circumstances.

sections.h: Beforehand: keep an information sheet ready
p: Include a recent photograph, physical description, important medication, communication method, usual places, contacts, vehicle registration or transport details where relevant, and any information that could help guide the search. Update it when the photograph or information changes.

Call 112 if there is immediate risk and report the disappearance without delay to Policía Nacional or Guardia Civil. Take the photograph and any available information. Do not delay reporting because of the mistaken idea that 24 hours must pass first.

AlertCops provides chat with Policía Nacional/Guardia Civil, an SOS button and location sharing with contacts; some ‘Guardián’ functions are activated for specific services or circumstances. It does not replace making a report and should not be presented as a system for permanently locating another person without their knowledge.

notaFuente: The II Plan Estratégico en materia de Personas Desaparecidas runs from 2026 to 2029, with funding of €5.1 million, five lines of action, thirteen objectives and 102 measures.

title: School and secondary school: support, adjustments, attendance and exams
lede: The LOE/LOMLOE requires specific educational support needs to be identified, resources to be provided, and inclusion and non-discrimination to be ensured. Specific support is also regulated by each autonomous community.

p: Access adjustments, communication support, changes of seating or location, breaks, advance preparation, technology, accessible materials, assessment adjustments, involvement from guidance services and individualised measures. The law covers needs related to disability, language and communication disorders, attention or learning, high ability and other circumstances.

Request a meeting with the tutor or guidance team and describe the barrier: ‘in a written exam they cannot finish because of reading speed’, ‘the dining hall causes overload’, ‘they cannot respond orally in this situation’. Ask what measure has been agreed, who will apply it and when it will be reviewed.

Persistent attendance difficulties need an investigation into what is happening: anxiety, bullying, overload, pain, sleep, learning, transport or conflict. Punishing absence without identifying the barrier can make it worse.

title: The Ministry grant for specific educational support needs (NEAE)
lede: This is the annual national call for grants and subsidies for pupils with specific educational support needs. It should always be published with the academic year, deadline and amounts for that year.

p: Applications are open from 08:00 on 19 May 2026 until 15:00 on 10 September 2026. Applications are submitted through the Ministry's electronic office. The Ministry states that these grants are incompatible with the general grant for post-compulsory studies.

The call covers different types of specific need and programmes for high-ability pupils. The exact requirements for disability, age, reports, income and type of support must be checked in the call for the relevant academic year; requirements from the previous year should not automatically be reused.

sections.h: The key point in the application
p: The report should relate to the support being requested. Before submitting the application, check that the documents specifically evidence the need for which transport, meals, educational support or another item is being requested.

title: Studying at university with support
lede: Spanish universities have services or units that support students with disabilities and accessibility needs. Specific adjustments depend on the evidenced need and on each university's rules and procedures.

p: Fundación ONCE's Guía Universitaria can be used to find, university by university, support services, accessibility resources, assistive products and adjustments to learning and assessment.

Measures may include extra time, accessible formats, room changes, technological support, adjustments to placements and coordination with teaching staff. There is no single automatic adjustment that applies identically to everyone with the same diagnosis.

Contact the support service before classes begin or as soon as the need arises. It is useful to provide any available report or certificate and, above all, explain the specific barrier: reading, writing, noise, attendance, timing, communication, mobility or assessment.
Ask for the response in writing and use the university's internal review or complaints procedures. Equal treatment and accessibility also apply to education.

title: Looking for work when you are neurodivergent
lede: Looking for work may require different support from what is needed once a person is employed. This entry brings together routes into employment and notes that disclosing a diagnosis during recruitment is not a general requirement.

p: In Spain, there are guidance and job-matching services specialising in disability and neurodivergence, as well as public employment services. Inserta Empleo (Fundación ONCE) works with people who have officially recognised disability; autism organisations and specialist programmes also provide training, guidance and contact with employers.

A readable CV, a brief explanation of strengths and tasks the person does well, specific examples of experience and a private list of adjustments that might be helpful. An interview does not need to become a clinical explanation.

Some employment measures and reserved schemes require an officially recognised degree of disability of 33% or more. Other ordinary vacancies do not. Check the requirement for each programme and do not assume that ‘neurodivergent’ and ‘officially recognised disability’ are administratively equivalent.

title: Reasonable adjustments at work
lede: Once someone is employed, the question is no longer ‘how do I get a job?’ but which changes allow them to do the job without an avoidable disadvantage.

p: Article 40 of RDL 1/2013 requires employers to take appropriate workplace adaptation and accessibility measures for disabled people unless doing so would impose an excessive burden.

Written instructions; fewer interruptions; headphones where compatible with safety; a quieter location; reasonable changes to working hours; remote working where the role and agreement allow it; a priority list; time for training; and adjustments to interviews or tests.

Describe the barrier, the proposed measure and how it makes it possible to do the job. There is no need to provide more clinical information than is necessary. Keep the request and response in writing.

title: Getting a driving licence when you are neurodivergent
lede: The DGT has accessibility measures for people with specific learning difficulties and disabilities. The current guide available on its website is the 3rd edition, October 2024.

p: The DGT recommends support for the theory and practical tests: clear and concise instructions, consideration of orientation or right/left difficulties, sufficient advance warning of manoeuvres, and measures to reduce reading and processing barriers. The specific arrangements are coordinated with the Jefatura and the test centre.

The driver assessment centre evaluates fitness under the Reglamento General de Conductores. A diagnosis on its own cannot automatically determine ‘fit’ or ‘unfit’; functioning, any required reports and the person's specific circumstances matter.

Give notice of the need for an adjustment in good time and bring the supporting documentation specified by the DGT. Do not wait until the day of the test to explain a barrier that requires advance organisation.

avisoFuente: The DGT guide is currently on its 3rd edition, dated October 2024. The edition number appears in the PDF path: when a new edition is published, it needs to be updated.

title: Going to the doctor, dentist or emergency department
lede: A healthcare appointment can be made more accessible by explaining in advance what will happen and reducing the burden of waiting, communication and sensory input. The person has the right to receive information they can understand and, if they have a disability, the support needed to take part in healthcare decisions.

p: The first or last appointment of the day; written instructions; warning before touch; step-by-step explanations; more time to respond; support from a trusted person if requested; reduced waiting; a less noisy space; and use of the person's own communication method.
Ley 41/2002 provides that, where the patient is a disabled person, support measures and information in appropriate formats must be offered to help them give consent for themselves.

A one-page sheet listing medication, allergies, communication method, signs of pain, what helps and what makes things harder. If the person uses AAC, take it charged and keep it available: it should not be removed because ‘today you need to talk to the doctor’.
Clinical safety comes first. Even so, tell triage staff about communication or sensory barriers that may make examination more difficult and about simple adjustments that can make it work better.
